The Stench of Demoniacs and the “Foetent.verbatim:
Another consequence of the inner dissolution is the smell which those initiated into these mysteries emit from their mouths and whole bodies; which thereupon communicates itself to their clothes, and transfers a pestilential stench onto all who come near them, and fills the houses, the air and all neighboring places so that it endures for a long time. In these words Brognoli has described the condition of the demoniacs; and the testimony of all exorcists agrees with this result. Not only is the whole body infected with this stench; every single secretion from the mucous membranes, the kidneys, &c., is marked by the same infection. Opposite the odor of holiness on the good side therefore stands, in full truth, the stench of unholiness; which proclaims itself so decisively that the elders accordingly called them the Foetentes, and the Gascons called them the Fetilléres. Just as the sweet scent of the saints tends to increase with every holy action they perform, so the stench of the unholy will increase and decrease with the degree of depravity to which they have sunk; and with each manifestation of them will only be concentrated.

We have ascribed that sweet scent to the production of an ethereal oil which develops in the simplified life-process, under the influence of a higher illumination, like the aromas in a blossom. The foul smell must therefore likewise be ascribed to the production of a putrid and inflammable animal oil, which is generated in the depressed life in the flames that burn through it; as the sharp and caustic or stupefying juices are produced under the sun's burning in poisonous plants. \[Page 148\]

Sharpened emanations tend already in ordinary life to accompany every deviation from moral harmony, which is immediately met by a corresponding natural dissonance; for the sharpened sense of the saints testifies to this, who, as we have seen, have smelled the sins of those who approached them, particularly the sins of the flesh; whereas the expression "stinking pride" seems to render this vice intelligible to the common understanding. A habitual intimacy with evil will therefore also render such a production permanent, and will thereby increase it both qualitatively and quantitatively so that no specially heightened sense is needed to perceive its presence; rather it forces itself upon ordinary powers of perception.

While, therefore, to the saints a conservative power is given which remains dominant even through frailty and sickness, and preserves in them the sweet odour even in conditions which otherwise unavoidably are associated with foul smell, yea even preserves them uncorrupted after death; in the demonic a destructive principle seizes, piercing even through their health: so that their healthy body already, like a cancerous ulcer, is foul-smelling, and, at death, rapid and swift dissolution and putrefaction follow. This is already hinted at in life by the uncleanness into which they must be brought; for the statements of many in their interrogations ran as follows: the unclean spirit does not allow them to wash themselves in the morning. It was therefore even believed that daily washing of the hands, and commending oneself to God's protection before going out, gave security against witchcraft; and Mugeta von Essem warned her husband earnestly about this, even before her burning at Remy.

The Attempted Abduction of Fana Haquart.verbatim:
Remy gives a clear example properly attested by witnesses, which we will cite from him here on account of its singularity. Franziska Haquart, who stood before the court in the year 1587, had, when her daughter Fana was only seven years old, given her over to the unclean spirit, so that he would thereafter leave her untroubled. She immediately reported this to the judge, and the daughter's testimony agreed with the mother's statement. On account of her youth she was released, while the mother had to atone with fire. A respectable matron thereupon took the child in hand and urged her to the fear of God, to bring her back from the godless condition. It succeeded so well that at last people entirely came to believe that it had been altogether accomplished. \[Page 150\]

Then it happened that, one night when she lay in bed between two maids, she was suddenly borne aloft, as if the spirit would take her with it. How likely --- it would indeed have actually happened --- had not the maids prevented it by their cry: "Lord Jesus, help!" When the spirit thus saw his work disturbed, he left his prey hanging up among the beams, and departed. The maids did not invent this; the whole neighborhood attested to what had occurred. For at the cry for help from the maids everyone hastened in and had seen how everything was arranged. The stiffness in which the little maid was found, her pitiable condition, and the fact that for eight whole days she took no food, remaining continually awake and silent, proved that no deceit had crept in. The very rigidity in which the child was found testifies that her condition had been nervous; that in the seizure she had spasmed locally, and was then borne aloft as far as the space permitted. What of demonical in the matter there may have been remained behind from the former direction which the mother had given the child, and was therefore accidental.

The Witch of Pamplona Who Flies from a T.verbatim: The Bishop of Pamplona, Pr. von Sandoval, relates in his History of Charles V, on the occasion of a witch-trial that was held before the royal council in Navarre, the following fact. He wished to satisfy himself by personal inspection as to the cause of the circumstances there occurring, and therefore promised clemency to an old witch, from among the others, if she would perform her sorcery in his presence. The old woman accepted the proposal and asked for her ointment-box, which had been taken from her; and then she, in the company of the commissioner and many other persons, climbed up a tower. There she placed herself at a window and, with the ointment, rubbed her flat hand, her loins, the joints of the elbow, the underside of the arm, the shoulder and the left side. Then she called with a loud voice: "Art thou present?" Everyone present then heard a voice in the air say: "Yes, here I am!" The witch then began to descend the tower, head downwards, using her hands and feet in the fashion of lizards. When she had thus reached about the middle of the height, she took flight into the air; and the eyes of those present followed her until the horizon hid the flyer. All remained full of astonishment at what they had seen, and the commissioner caused it to be announced that a considerable sum of money would be given to whoever should bring the escaped woman back. After two days the shepherds brought in the one found. The commissioner asked her why she had not flown farther away in order to escape the inquiries of those searching for her. She answered that her master had only undertaken to conduct her three hours' distance, and had then left her in the field where the shepherds found her. Llorente relates in his History of the Inquisition the course of this affair, which ended with whipping and several years' imprisonment for the 150 participants involved. \[Page 151\]

Two Peasants Found Hanging in Trees Afte.verbatim: Thus Rémy relates from his records: Once, in the German Vosges, near Huncaria, a violent storm arose with thunder and lightning; the shepherds, for protection against the tempest, had withdrawn with their cattle into the woods. There they suddenly saw two peasants hanging high up in the tree-tops, and their minds were so stunned and distraught that one could clearly see they had not climbed there intentionally but had arrived by some accident. The state of their clothing, covered with dirt as if they had been dragged over stick and stone, meanwhile aroused the suspicion that demonic force had placed them in the trees; and this seemed to be confirmed when, after they had sat there for a while and no one was watching them, they came down and vanished. Afterwards arrested, they freely confessed what the shepherds had asserted of them.

Rothar and Amantius Falling from a Cloud.verbatim: Likewise, once in Bellmont during a storm two men --- a certain Rothar and another called Amantius --- fell from a cloud onto a roof. The first had expressed great concern in that position about how they might come safely to the ground; the other, however, had replied laughingly, "Be calm, fool! for he who has us in his power can do still more." And indeed they were seized by a whirl and forthwith brought down to the earth uninjured; whereby the whole house trembled so that it seemed shaken to its foundations. The inhabitants were all unanimous in their testimony as to the circumstances and the day on which it happened.

Margaretha Warma Set Down on an Oak by a.verbatim: Again, Cunin, a magistrate of Roncas, in December 1586 had been attending to business out on the meadow; and since the sky proved very stormy, he set out in haste for home. Suddenly a lightning strike had uprooted six oaks around him, and a seventh, which had remained standing, was torn and riven as if by claws. As he now hurried home all the more, having only lost his hat, he saw on the top of the oak a woman who seemed to have been set down there from the cloud. He recognized her, and called to her: Are you the ill-famed Margaretha Warma, upon whom, as I now see, suspicion of witchcraft has not been groundless; how then have you come here? She answered: Conceal what you have now seen; no smallest ill shall from me befall you and yours in the future! Cunin swore to his statement before the judge, and Warma confirmed it by her confession, without the use of torture, and at the last moment.

The Naked Woman Who Falls from a Cloud a.verbatim: Del Rio relates a fourth case as equally beyond doubt. He was at Calais in 1587, when Archduke Albert took the town; on the bridge toward Boulogne, where the enemy lay, the Walloon outposts were posted. Two of them saw in the evening, under a clear sky, a blackish cloud approach; and heard confused voices issue from it, without being able to distinguish anything. Because they mistrusted the matter, one fired his arquebus; and then a drunken, naked, rather stout woman of middle age, wounded, fell from the cloud at their feet, who acted foolishly and could hardly say anything but: Are enemies or allies about here? \[Page 152\]

The Peasant’s Vision of a Vast Nocturnal.verbatim:
If the impulse to hover seizes simultaneously many who are connected in demonic rapport, and if these impulses are all directed to the same distant goal, to the place of the Sabbath, then thereby the excursion will be formed; and the next question must now arise: are the participants in this excursion bodily and physical, in real locomotive movement, to that place, or are they present there only outwardly in appearance and in a spiritual manner; that is, are they present in the one place without being at the same time present at the other, distant place? Some have accepted both kinds of presence, and in order to prove the reality of the former have repeatedly adduced facts which, as invented out of the air, can be dismissed; rather, a more exact inquiry is required. The two most important \[cases\] to us here must be those that Fr. Bartholomew de Spina has set forth in his book. An eminent physician of Ferrara, who in that city is especially devoted to the care of the poor sick, called Sozinus Bentius, has in the last days told me the following with the most sincere truthfulness.

He said that three years ago he had been in the country to look after his estates, and there he had by chance fallen into a conversation with his farmer about the witches. The physician had maintained that all that is told about them is mere imagination; especially, he said, if one believes that they physically set out on the ride. The farmer, however (who is still living and is called Thomasinus Pollastros, born indeed in the district of Mirandula, but now residing in that neighborhood in the place called Clavica Malaguzzi), answered that he knew a peasant who lived nearby and who himself, with his own eyes, by night had seen men and women in great numbers who danced and gave themselves up to all manner of lusts. The doctor was astonished at this remark and begged his bailiff to bring that peasant to him. He came, and, when asked about the matter, gave the following account. \[Page 153\]

One night, when I had risen three hours before dawn in order to bring my oxen and my cart to my tenant to assist him in some business, and had thereby come to that plain to which he pointed with his hand because it lay near, I saw from afar many fires in different places, like great lights; and between them a great multitude of men and women who as it were quarrelled among themselves, or else danced together. But when I came nearer I beheld, in the bright light which the fires shed around them, more than six thousand people; and there were tables set up at which many sat and made merry with food and drink; several danced and practised various games; others took out things about which it is indecorous to speak at greater length. Among the crowd I saw some men and women already known to me, and I spoke with several. But after an hour all rose at a certain signal, hurried away, and vanished as if in a mist.

On this testimony the physician changed his opinion, and held that what he had formerly declared to be delusion was not only possible but really did occur. The same author reports: Brother Paulus of Caspan of his order assured him that a priest, J. Ant. von Palavisinis, an honorable man who lives at Caspani in the Veltlin, had told him the following. When, before dawn, he rises as usual to perform divine service or to attend to other business, it has often happened to him that he has seen a great number of men and women in a neighboring plain running about with lights as if in play, and he has recognized them as witches and sorcerers in their assembly.

The Sabine Peasant Anointed and Led to t.verbatim: Many other narratives circulate concerning such gatherings, said to have been held truly and bodily, remote from human intercourse, into which eyewitnesses accidentally stumbled. Besides the fact that in these reports it is never clearly shown whether what was seen was not either merely too corporeal, or not rather a vision, all these accounts lack the external authenticity that would be required to admit them as testimonial evidence. There is the peasant from the Sabine country, near Rome, whom his wife persuaded to anoint himself. He is at once led under the walnut tree near Benevento, where he finds many gathered who eat and drink and make merry. He does as the others; but since the unsalted dishes do not please his taste, he repeatedly asks for salt. He finally receives what he demanded, and then says: "Praise be to God, now that this salt has come." Immediately everything falls apart, the spell vanishes, and the man is left alone. He must painfully beg his way home; he then accuses his wife along with others whom he had seen there; they confess and are all burned. Grillandus, who relates the story in the first book of his work De sortilegiis, gives no names and adduces no witnesses; but even if the matter were best investigated on that side, it would not prove what it sets out to prove. For the peasant had been anointed, and thus was subject to all the enchantments that commonly accompany that condition.

Bertranda of Forbach and the Sleeping Hu.verbatim:
The women who rode out used to put the men at their sides to sleep by applying the salve, so as not to be disturbed by them in their proceedings. Bertranda, the barber's wife in Forbach, confessed that on such occasions she, with her anointed right hand, plucked at her companion's ear, whereupon he then fell asleep. Exactly the same thing occurs in the trial of the witch of Loches in Bodin, who calls it a matter still quite fresh in memory. She and her husband are transported from Loches to the heaths of Bordeaux, fifteen days' journey away. The husband says: "My God, where are we?" Immediately everything scatters; there is a trial, and the woman confesses everything without coercion. Thus in the year 1525 a girl from the duchy of Spoleto, thirteen years old, is led in by a witch; the girl, amazed at all she sees, cries out: "Blessed God, what is this?" Everything has vanished; in the morning a peasant finds her in the field.

Torquemada, in the third book of his work, relates: a sorcerer persuades a man to ride with him, and the latter consents. He then takes him by the hand, and they fly through the air very far off. There they find the Sabbath assembled. But the newcomer loses patience and cries out: "God --- what a great noise!" Immediately a whirlwind and a storm break in, and everything is scattered. It takes him three years before he comes back to his native place.

Witches Leaving Pillows, Brooms, and Spe.verbatim: By the same line of reasoning it once happened that, in a distinguished city in Germany, the authorities were deceived so far as to hang an innocent locksmith because his lock-picks had been found at a place where money had been stolen from a chest. But another had taken his lock-picks and used them, which he afterwards confessed. Yes, some --- those who ought to admonish judges to fairness and leniency --- are so perverse toward the poor man: when the husband testifies about his wife that she was on that night, the very night she is said to have been at the dance and to have been seen there, never out of bed and lying on his side, then they say and argue: in the bed lay a specter, but the true body had been outside. Dear sirs, why do you not invert this and interpret it --- not to the devil's discredit, but for the good of man --- so that the true body lay in bed and the false one was outside? Is it not a principle with you that, in doubtful matters, one should always prefer the milder to the harsher? --- One must say there is good and sound common sense in these words. Meanwhile many of the accused themselves had voluntarily sworn: they had left their child's pillows in the bed in their place; others a broom, a scarecrow, or even their own spirit as a succubus.

The Spirit Who Repeatedly Abducted the C.verbatim:
The age that entertained such an excess of belief that the ordinary, prosaic world thereby stood in danger of disappearing in the same way as the invisible world is in danger now through present unbelief, accepted this account without the smallest doubt. What Binsfeld, an upright and very reliable man, relates from the Trier records may well demonstrate the possibility of such real abductions; but it does not suffice to establish the reality of such assemblies. He adduces, first, a noteworthy example of an invisible child-abduction to prove the power of imperceptible forces in the matter. The wife of Johann Eysenkopf, a burgher of Wilmar, called Margaretha, had borne a little boy named Conrad. A spirit often stole him from the cradle, before and after her laying-out \[i.e. the funeral-like rite?\] --- from the feast of the Resurrection to that of the Departure of the Apostles --- and carried him to other places. Once he laid him in the mother's bed, another time he hid him beneath the steps of the cellar-stair; at times he carried him to the loft or to the privy. But so that no harm should befall the child in these happenings, he always placed cloths under him which he had likewise secretly stolen from the parents.

Once, when the mother destroyed such a bed as the spirit had prepared in the bathing-room, her face and hands swelled up, as far as they were not covered by her clothes, and her skin peeled off. At times the spirit would also rock the little boy, and he always cried when his mother had put him into the cradle, but was perfectly calm when the spirit had carried him to another place. The dean of the place, W. Lyndner, wrote to Binsfeld for remedy, and the latter advised the use of sacramentals. They were applied, and the older people also undertook a pilgrimage, whereupon the matter subsided for a time. But soon the consecrated objects were found torn away, and the invisible one began his game again. All that was told had, at the dean's request, been authentically recorded by the local notary. \[Page 158\]

Michael of Longen, Martin of Corlingen,.verbatim: Binsfeld then relates further. On 22 September 1589 the peasant Michael from Longen, in the Amt of Pfalzel, was executed for witchcraft; he confessed among other things that he had been led at Christmas to the Sabbath at the cross of Longwich, on this side of the Moselle, but had only arrived there after the dispersal of the assembly. Thereupon he cried out, "Lord God, it is already over!" In the same instant he had fallen down into the field, and about eleven o'clock at night had gone to the Moselle, put himself into a boat across the stream, and gone to bed. In the year 1591, on 4 May, Martin of Corlingen was burned there; he confessed that twice, on the return from the Sabbath, he had been thrown into the bushes near Pellingen because he had said, "O God, how did we come to be here?" Once, he said, when during the dearth he had bought a sack of wheat in the town, he had been carried over the wall together with the purchase. Anna Meisenbein of Cologne had gone to the assembly on the Hetzenrodter heath; after its conclusion she quarrelled with her daughter and beat her in the presence of her son. The mother, the daughter, and the son had all given this account in complete agreement.

The Oostbruck Servant with Dislocated Fe.verbatim: Only a few related cases: for example, where the servant of a woman in Oostbruck, in the reed-swamp, was found with his feet dislocated, whom his wife had thrown down during Ascension; she, being taken in and examined by Judge J. Culemberg of Utrecht, confessed the matter without evasion. This and some similar occurrences seem to indicate that in rare cases, as a consequence of a specific lightness (a levity) occurring in demonic states, just as in ecstatic ones, such sorties may indeed take place.

Maria d’— of Handaye and the Greenish Oi.verbatim: The critical days of the Sabbath are well known to the initiated; they therefore urge one another not to miss the gathering, and are also sometimes admonished by their spirits. In earlier times much is also said of the noise of the procession which, led by its queen, swept past the houses of the laggards and reminded them to join. They anoint themselves when they still require it, or when it pleases them so to do; but those who have attained greater practice need it in no way --- as many examples shown in the arrested, and many witness statements, attest. The ointment was rubbed on the naked body, sometimes also applied to the clothes, which nevertheless appeared no less clean and neat on the Sabbath. Maria d'--- of Handaye had testified against Mariacho de Moleres: when they wished to set out, she had anointed her hands, loins and knees with a thick, greenish water, and the witness then, seizing her, led her away. One sees that each must either have been in that same state of ecstasy, or the anointing itself must already have belonged to her. Occasionally already a very lively desire is sufficient to produce the rapture.

Catharina de Landalde’s Irresistible Lon.verbatim: Catharina de Landalde, thirty years old, from the parish of Ustaritz, confessed that when she sat in the evening by the fire such a desire came upon her to go to the Sabbath that she had never felt so violent and irresistible a longing for anything as at that time. She then always went there on foot, without any sleep, dreams, or illusions having been produced in her, nor could any doubt arise in her about the reality of what she had seen. It is readily seen that in her a favourable disposition had been well formed by long practice; only an instantaneous, scarcely perceptible passage through the sleep-state was required, and she awoke inwardly with such clearness of what was seen that, as she with equal swiftness passed into the waking state, the memory of what had been seen, likewise without visible transition, attached itself to the circle of ideas of the new sphere.

Maria de Ralde and the Swift Foot-Journe.verbatim: The going on foot, as it showed itself in her, is moreover the one and first type of outing. Maria de Ralde, twenty-eight years old, confessed that she sometimes, in the company of all her neighbours, went to the Sabbath on foot. They then advanced so swiftly as if they had flown, and in a moment arrived at the place. Each time, when she thus found herself united with her companions, she felt a marvellous contentment; for the devil binds the will of those who have been in the assembly only once or twice so firmly that no other desire or longing easily comes to equal it. Other accounts by such persons, who in this way went to the Sabbath or returned from it leading children by the hand, confirmed this information. They were conscious of all the circumstances of their going, which people they met, whom they called upon; and all together affirmed the full reality and corporality of the perceptions they had experienced. But this was not only the case in the Basque country, but elsewhere as well. The Lotharingian women of Pangra likewise asserted that they always went on foot; only when they came to a body of water did the spirit carry them across. If Satan was present there, he as a rule appears as the guide of the travelling witch-women. He summons them or has them summoned at the appointed hour; those who happen to be asleep are inwardly awakened, and then behold the leader in the form of a horse, ass, ox, pig, poodle or billy-goat, and sometimes of a bird, which takes them upon its back. At times even that is unnecessary; any object to which the vision can attach itself---a stick or broom, a spindle-distaff, a pitchfork, anointed or unanointed---already suffices. Sometimes they imagine themselves winged and skim over wide countries. Sometimes only the crown of the head is anointed; children taken by the armpits must sit in front and are carried in that way. Occasionally several of those bound in closer fellowship mount the same pack-beast, and it then proceeds with the cry: "Up on and nowhere!" into the air; most beloved is it in the smoke of the element which, among all, by its nature rises upward from their hearth; sometimes, however, it also goes from some crossroads to which they repair. If meanwhile rain falls, the cry among the Welsh---"Haut la coude Quillet!"---causes the beast with its tail to shield the carried ones from all wetting. The crowing of the night watch and the early morning messenger is exceedingly hateful to the riders; nothing can be more hostile and vexatious to them than his cry when it rings in the ears of those prepared for the ride. Likewise hostile to them are the ringing of bells, and the utterance of the name "Jesu" likewise breaks the charm. Yet the outing must by no means be regarded as effortless; for those led in it grow so weary as if they had traversed a long, rough road on foot; and Barbara Ragel often had to keep her bed for three days after such a journey, and could not stand on her feet.

Judicial Testimonies of Metamorphosis, F.verbatim:
Jeannette of Belloc, twenty-four years old, who had been present at the Sabbath since early youth, related: it is there like at a fair. Many walked about in human shapes; others were transformed into dogs, cats, asses, horses, pigs. Yet she added that she had never been able to learn the manner of this transformation, and had only seen all those animals running about there; they could also, at will, make themselves very small, and again as tall as houses.

Jeannette d'Abadie, however, testified how she had been present when this one and that one were transformed into a wolf, a dog, etc.; how they washed their hands in a water which they had kept in a pot with them. They would then at pleasure resume their former shape; and all this not only on the Sabbath, but on the way to it and everywhere. They thereupon vanished so that one saw only a shimmer of them. Both witnesses agreed: there is a constant coming and going; some flew up into the air; others still higher heavenward, while others settled lower down on the land. Some plunged into kindled fires like rockets or lightning; they also went in crowds to do this, and on return related how they had been in Newfoundland within the past two or three hours; how they had sat upon the mast of this or that ship, but could not step aboard because it had been blessed; instead, there they raised a storm in the rigging. They had seen all their own beyond, and which of their relations, who were notoriously in America, had been in their company.

Abbé Rousseau’s Attack by a Toad and Res.verbatim: Abbe Rousseau relates in the tenth section of his Remed Secretorum how he had kept one of these animals enclosed in a glass, with the intention of letting it die in its prison, as he had already done with some others. Once, after watching for a while the most strenuous efforts the toad made to get out, it suddenly turned upon him, rose up, swelling itself in an extraordinary way, lifted itself up on its legs to a great height; and then blew, without moving from its place, around itself. The enraged creature looked at him with eyes that, imperceptibly, seemed to become quite red and fiery, so that in that very moment a weakness came over him which made him swoon. A cold sweat ensued, and a flux set in, both of the bowels and of the urine; and his condition was such that his people thought him dead and lost.

The Soissons Priest, the Baptized Toad,.verbatim: Peter Grey of Toulouse already relates: an unhappy priest from the diocese of Soissons had asked a witch in what manner he might most effectually take revenge on his enemies, and she had advised him: to baptize a toad under the name of John, and then cause it to eat a consecrated host. After that he was to tear it apart, and might prepare from it a poison that would bring death to all his enemies; which indeed happened. The affair was discovered, and she was handed over to the flames. That took place in the year 1460. Therefore it is these creatures that form the flock of the Sabbath. There they are herded by children at a brook, to whom a white rod is given for the purpose. The animals are clothed in red or white velvet, have a small bell at the neck, and sometimes on the feet; and witnesses testified that they had seen the daughter of the Lady of Martibelsarena dancing at the Sabbath with four such animals; she carried one so clothed on her left shoulder, an unclothed one on the right, and two similar ones on her fists, like a huntsman his hawks.

Hermit Dominicus’s Daily Visions of Drag.verbatim:
Herbert, a contemporary of St. Bernard --- round whom a whole world of visions disclosed itself --- tells us something like this of a friend of his youth, the hermit Dominicus. He had formerly lived in the Cistercian monastery Carrezeda near León, and was then dismissed by the abbot into solitude, dwelling near that city in a mountain cave, practising the strictest continence; almost shut off from all intercourse with the world, devoting himself to contemplation; burning with love of God, and in a wonderful way endowed with the gift of tears.

Once he sat at the entrance of his cave, his gaze turned toward heaven, attentively following the light of a sunbeam to its source. Suddenly he perceived the shape of a burning dragon, which, descending in that very ray, in a violent plunge threw itself toward his face as if to devour it. Terrified by the apparition, he crouched inward; called on the Lord, and made the sign of the cross against the assailant. Driven off, it was yet able to do nothing against him, but it flew constantly about him and would not leave him. He then shut his eyes and covered his face with his garments; but that availed him nothing, for he saw the figure with closed eyelids as though with them open; and this penetrating, subtle being could not be repelled by clothing. When he saw, therefore, that he could not escape the sight, he opened his eyes again, and let them behold that whose attack he could not prevent. Then other demons likewise came to light in serpent form and other animal shapes, in hordes, and filled the dwelling from top to bottom.

Among them there was so great a diversity of dimensions, such variation in their properties, and such ugliness in their forms that it cannot be described, and many of them were fire-colored. They swarmed about him like bees, flared up like fire in a thorn-bush, dashing at him with angry movements and attacking him with blows. But although they appeared fiery, they by no means had the power to burn. For though they flew around him in a circle, and, sweeping past him at the swiftest speed, often struck his face, they did indeed press upon him in every way, but never harmed him with fire. When he then again went out somewhat before the door, to breathe somewhat from the oppression; there also appeared to him whole heaps of demons, in great swarms traversing the air, and filling everything from the earth to the heaven. These too were so manifoldly graded, so terrible through their extraordinary appearance, so gruesome through their ugliness: that human senses could not endure such a confluence of monsters, had not the power of Heaven assisted them. \[Page 166\]

He shared with me at that time the observation: these impure spirits had not laid aside the spiritual forms in which they always appeared to him in the air before the sign of the cross; but rather those into which they had fantastically transformed themselves. From then on, until the day of writing it down, the man of God saw these visions daily while awake; both in daylight and in the nocturnal darkness, with closed eyes just as with open. But the terror and the distress which he had at first entirely vanished; so that in the end he made no more of them than if they were flies or other vermin. For the light-spirits also visited him, and filled him with their consolations; however, about their forms he never, out of discretion,

Maria de Ralde’s Vision of Satan as Tree.verbatim:
Let us see what the judicial testimonies about these types report to us: varying, as is comprehensible, in the apprehension of them, according to the turbidity or clarity of the beholding.

Maria de Ralde, who since her tenth year had visited the Sabbath, but for five years had given up the abomination, testified: she had there seen the Satan for the first time in the form of a tree stump, without feet. He seemed to sit on a chair, with something that looked like a human face, but as if covered with darkness. From there downward she saw him more clearly, in the form of a man, either of red or black color. Usually it is a stone that stands in the middle of the place, on which the one whom they call the Lord or also the Master sits.

Beside that tree-like form, like an old cypress or oak struck by lightning, and dried up from the top downward, it is now especially the form of the goat that he loves to assume. But if he appears in human form, then he presents himself in the form of a tall, black man, red and flaming like a fire that bursts from the oven, whose forms appear only halfway; with a broken, inarticulate, but commanding, noisy and terrible voice; often done in such a way that it is hard to distinguish whether it is man, animal, or tree trunk. He sits in a chair, apparently gilded, but glowing; the queen of the Sabbath, whom he has taken for himself from the initiates, in all splendor and glory at his side. Everything around, persons and things, appears in a false nothing; all forms in the enormous, gigantic or dwarfed and shifted. Jeanette d'Abadie saw him with six, sometimes eight horns, a long tail, and a double face. Sometimes there are two of them present: a Grand Master Leonard, and a smaller one, whom the Basques called Master Jean Mullin, and whom the former, in his absence, substituted in his place.

Descriptions of Lesser Demons Serving at.verbatim:
Beside this Master, however, there are still many other demons of every order present in the lodge; and indeed, as one who belonged to the higher ones testified, more in number than humans. They undertake manifold tasks, set the tables, procure all necessities, consort with men and women as succubi and incubi, serve as cupbearers, assist at the sacrifice, transform themselves into animals, manage the musical exercises at the Sabbath, and as attendants are often assigned to the women in the form of toads. Many of the latter had closely observed these their spirits, and said of them: they had a dark, black face, deep eyes sparkling like flames; a wide, deep, always foul-smelling maw, exhaling like a sulfurous vapor; rough, hairy hands with sharp claws; feet with cloven hooves, and in their shape always without proportion, either too small or too large, and otherwise without all measure.

Aleria Belhora of Blamweiler saw them sometimes without a head, sometimes with only one foot. These spirits, although according to another account they know many languages, yet always speak in the vernacular; and from it are also taken the names which they bear: Misfortune, Torment, Featherbrush etc. in German; among the Romance speakers, however: maistre persil, Solybois, Verdelet, Sautebuisson. But their voice too has something artificially made about it; three witnesses compared it to a sound coming forth from a barrel or a broken pot, small, soft, lisping. They are at the beginning quite kind and pious, and accustom one well to the like. To Mallot his one advises: to abstain from gluttony, unchastity and every wrong; he should always keep God before his eyes, give alms, fast twice a week, and not forget his daily prayer.

Homage to the Goat-Shaped Master: Kissin.verbatim:
If the Sabbath in the relation first described was a cookshop of the evil principle and the Venus mountain, whither the inflamed life pressed to enter as a guest with the food master, and to intoxicate itself in lust from his beaker; then the scene now passes over into the throne room of the imperial palace. The emperor, or his plenipotentiary, sits crowned on a golden seat, the chosen empress at his side; and the estates of the realm appear, to present their homage and to obtain investiture. But here the contradiction that lies in the whole relation steps forth most glaringly, and manifests itself in the sharpest irony. On the throne sits a goat or a goatish figure; for the inner essence will not and cannot hide itself. Just as the good fragrance in such an atmosphere yields place to the stench, so every beauty to ugliness. Where the immoderate holds sway, there can be no question of measured bearing, dignity and majesty; the opposite of all that is therefore demanded there by the circumstances. The homage will thus also be, in its forms, a sarcastic parody of all submission to the higher; nevertheless, it will express the surrender into the blindest servitude. The act of homage is fulfilled as the homage-payers kiss the posterior and anterior parts of the goat.

The face of man is held upright, his eye drinks in the light, his ear the sound-ether; while his mouth inhales the air, and in the exhaled air inscribes the thought in the word. Extremely characteristic is it that the goat-figure of the evil spirit is assigned a second face, turned downward; initiated into the night-realms of the depths; closely connected with all the excretory organs that open downward, and with all the paths through which life purifies itself in the refuse. On the middle of this face the kiss is pressed; and the kisser thereby pledges himself to eternal servitude under the absolutism of evil.

All who newly enter the circle---whether as children introduced into it by their mothers and relatives; whether already grown and led up for the first time by an earlier initiate---must begin by performing this homage. It repeats itself with all of them in every great celebration, which opens with this hand-kiss and only admits the most intimate to the kiss of the mouth. Every one who enters approaches the chair with fear and trembling, falls at the master's feet, and embraces his hips with humility; or all kneel before him with their backs turned to him, hands clasped together behind, and remain in this position until he bids them rise.

All who have performed the homage in such a manner have unanimously confessed: that once they have surrendered themselves to the devil, there is no more separation from him, and that their apostasy is punished with severe penalty; wherefore none of them ever dares to escape his tyranny. He indeed promises in all things the opposite of the Sermon on the Mount of the Savior: riches to the poor, joy to the sorrowful, power to the weak, beauty to the ugly, knowledge to the ignorant. The banquets were, on the first level, boisterous orgies for indulgence, in which the initiates debauched with their initiators. Now, on the third level, they become sacrificial meals, where their god breaks the bread for his worshippers, and offers the cup to the confederates after pronouncing the curse over it; so that, having partaken in this supper of his substance, and now appropriating it to themselves, they may be transubstantiated into the same, and no longer permitted to depart from him.

According to Del Rio, the meal was always opened with the formula that served as the prayer before the table: *En nom de Belzebub nostre grand maistre, souverain Commandeur et seigneur, noz viandes, boire et manger soyent garnis et munis pour noz refections, plaisirs et voluptez!* whereupon all chorused: *Ainst soit il!* When the banquet was ended, it was said: *De nostre refection salutaire prinse et veceue nostre Commandeur seigneur ei maistre Belzebub soit loué, gracié et remercié a son exaltation et commun bien!* whereupon the chorus again responded: *Ainsi soit il!*

In the ancient love-feast, it was the wine, from the vine of mildly radiant sun, distilled into the blood of the earth asceticized through cultivation; thus purified in the process of vegetation, and cleansed once more of all its dregs in the process of fermentation, and now gentle, enspiriting, and uplifting, it was held as the symbolic bearer of the higher life-spirit, who bleeds out in death for the race. But in these unlovely gatherings, it is the drink that makes one drunken and raging; sprung from that vine planted in volcanic soil, and in the ash of earthly Solfatara; and, in Egyptian intimation, the heart-blood of the giants, which, when they fell in wild combat, flowed onto the earth, was absorbed; and now it is the fitting expression of the evil that sprouts forth in the sun's blaze, from the earth impregnated with wickedness. \[Page 181\]

This is therefore the potion that the woman on the beast offers to the peoples in the cup; from which the princes drink, and in which the peoples intoxicate themselves. As they now, instead of the mild food of earlier times---milk and honey---choose for their nourishment the milk of the euphorbias, and the honey that drove the Romans, who found it in the Caucasus, to madness: so is their bread not taken from pure, healthy wheat; but from such as has been struck by ergot, smut, and rust, and which therefore holds death and destruction enclosed within itself. Poison and death and putrefaction are thus the signature of the substances in which the Eucharist of Satan is consummated; and which, now taken up into the inner circle of life, unite and bind it with that in whose remembrance they are celebrated. But union on this side is separation on the other; and the Eucharist of Hell, first consummated in the Fall of Man, binds itself to the profanation of that other Eucharist, celebrated in the fruits of the Tree of Life. Hence the blasphemous abominations performed with it on the Sabbaths. A woman confessed in 1457, amid many tears and sighs, in a public avowal before a great multitude of people: how she, for thirty years in succession, had each time secretly removed from her mouth the host received in the Easter communion, and then trampled it underfoot. The same had a priest done with the host consecrated by him; and when he was now led to the stake, he demanded that a cross be erected at the place where he had done it, and along the path by which he was conducted.

Whatever, therefore, the most dissolute madness in lust can devise; whatever a burning sensuality may drive up from its depths; whither unbridled passions, staggering, can lose themselves in delusion; the irremediable doom before which Nature herself recoils: all this is performed and practiced there as service to the new god. The wanton dances are therefore now sacrificial dances; in them death draws near to life, that he may court it; in ever narrower circles they swing around each other, and as the circles interweave themselves into a net, joy enkindles itself ragingly in pain. Sister Margaretha of the Holy Sacrament was thus, in her twelfth year, overtaken by violent convulsions, followed by a twelve-day state of half-sleep. Then a frightful condition came over her, from which only the laying on of a scapular freed her. Soon there followed such a heaviness in all her limbs that she could no longer hold herself on her feet, and, lying on the bed, could not move any of her leaden-heavy limbs; so that for seven to eight days she could scarcely take any food to herself. Then again, since all the doctors' remedies proved ineffective, violent convulsions followed. In this state one heard her call out with the accent of an enraptured soul: Let me regain my strength before the most holy Sacrament! The sisters resolved, upon her repeated cry, to carry the sick one into the choir; but when they tried to take the suppliant into their arms, none was able to lift her alone; only the strongest among them could at last, with unspeakable effort, bring her to the place. As soon as she had arrived at the door of the choir, there came, like a shining cloud from the tabernacle, which enveloped her and drove out the spirits. The cloud not only restored strength to her body, but made it so agile that she was sometimes carried from the choir door, at other times even from the cloister gate, as far as the altar railing. A wonderful peace descended upon her, and she, who through her illness had also lost the use of her sight, yet saw the object of her longing when it was exposed.

Once the efficacy of the remedy was known, they brought her from time to time into the choir and let her remain there for 3--4 hours; when she then returned to the sickroom, all her sufferings immediately returned. The doctors attributed her ills to a congestion of evil humors in the brain, and applied cupping to her head against it; she endured everything with the greatest resignation, although she well recognized the uselessness of the procedure. They then wanted to provide an outlet for the fluids between the skull and the brain membrane through trepanation. It was done, but no fluid nor vapor could be seen: everything was perfectly sound and healthy. This determined the superior, a wise and virtuous woman, to make a trial with obedience. In the convent was preserved the little cloak of the saintly Cardinal de Bérulle; this she laid upon her with the words: My sister, be healthy out of obedience to our most revered father! Immediately her convulsions ceased, which upon its return happened several times with the same success. At last the superior spoke the words: Be completely healthy in obedience, without convulsions, ravings, and blindness, and eat unhindered like the others. Immediately she was freed from all her ills, and henceforth ate without discomfort, as the doctors attested with official certificates.

Very instructive and significant is what occurred in the convent of Louviers regarding such things. As a result of the errors and confusions there, many nuns had become possessed; they were exorcised, and from the statements of their spirits it emerged that Picard had applied six different kinds of magic within the convent. One was composed to keep the nuns in constant discord; another, to awaken in their hearts a disordered inclination toward Picard and la Bavent; the third, to shake their chastity; the fourth, to awaken in them an inner aversion to faith, hope, and love, and to provoke blasphemies against God in them; the fifth, to arouse in them a desire for the Sabbath and all magic; the sixth, to produce in them a contempt and abhorrence toward all sacraments. They now continued the exorcisms to compel them to indicate the places where they were hidden, and to bring them to light. \[Page 202\]

The sorely pressed ones at last found themselves compelled to obey; and a great multitude of persons drawn together were eyewitnesses as they were truly found in their hiding places, and authentic verbal protocols were drawn up concerning it. On 14 June 1643, in accordance with the declaration of the spirit in Sister Maria of the Holy Sacrament, who called himself Putiphar, in the evening between 7 and 8 in her chamber, from a wooden paneling of the walls that had never seemed to be opened, the first was drawn forth. The second, the last among those enumerated above, was found on the 30th of July under the high altar six feet deep under the earth. On the 19th in the evening at half eleven a third in the sacristy, from the same depth; and on the 24th of August at half twelve in the cloister between the four doors a fourth. On the 8th of September at eight o'clock in the evening another followed, nine feet deep under the pillar of the new building, brought to light in the presence of the Archbishop of Toulouse. Again two others on the epistle and gospel sides of the altar, from a depth of 6 to 8 feet; and yet a tenth on the 1st of December between 1 and 2 after midnight, in the interior of the choir, near the door; from a place that had more than twelve feet of depth. An eleventh and a twelfth then came still on the 22nd of January, and were drawn to the light from a depth of more than 7 feet, directly under the image of the Holy Virgin in her chapel,

The possessed now spoke with wonder, concerning all these magic instruments, those who had indicated their place even before they were found, circumstantially of their composition, of the inscriptions under which they had been fabricated on the Sabbath; they gave all their components, the ligatures and knots applied to them, the letters with which they were marked, and all other circumstances, without ever erring in the smallest detail. Before one began to dig, they designated some spot on the floor, and indicated: directly perpendicular beneath it, in a depth of 6 to 7, 8 to 9 up to 12 feet, the magic lay. One proceeded accordingly in digging, and always found it at the spot indicated by the exorcism. They stated: some were marked with the letters M. P. and M. B., the names of Picard and of Bavent; they testified that at a certain place lay the testament of David and Picard written in the Arabic language of the Sabbath; and everything was found exactly at the place they had indicated. No one could read and understand the writing; but the two nuns who had attested their presence read it one after the other, word for word, and explained it in agreement

When she and some others, who afterward came into the same state with her, went to Communion; then they saw the grating toward the church illuminated with torches, but pursued by all sorts of phantoms, which, after frightening them greatly, flew off through the chimney. To Sister Maria de St. Nicolas came a phantom in the form of Picard, at about the time of sunrise, sat upon her bed, and spoke to her; while at another time, amid great noise, all sorts of utensils were overturned around her. She saw a phantom in terrible forms that stood motionless before her the whole night in her cell; if she went anywhere, it hurried ahead of her; in the choir it performed all sorts of juggling tricks before her to amuse her; and threatened her fiercely when she discovered the matter to the superior, who advised her to treat all the spook with contempt. At the time when she performed any act of humility and renunciation, the form fled; but upon returning, made what had happened ridiculous. During Mass it gaped its maw against the assembled, and threatened to devour them; set naked people before her, and sometimes struck them hard as well. When she sang with the others in the choir, she was often lifted a cubit high; and when others, to prevent this, placed their feet on hers, they felt these themselves lifted. Female convents will thus first be the scenes of such occurrences, and indeed there is no lack of examples where such things have taken place in such conventual associations. Among these cases there is especially one that was exactly and sharply observed by four bishops and four doctors of the Sorbonne; which they then likewise sharply weighed and discussed in its various circumstances; and concerning which, after they had confirmed the individual facts through repeated experiments, excluded the doubtful, and retained only what was evidently certain, they then drew up the following clear and luminous report, which dispels all suspicion of fraud and deception, and presents the matter roundly and plainly.

It reads, however, as follows: We, the undersigned, after having heard the report made to us by His Episcopal Grace of Châlons-sur-Saône concerning the occurrences that took place in his presence among many persons, some ecclesiastical, some secular, who seemed to be plagued and seized by the evil spirit, in Auxonne; at that time when, by order of the King and on the commission of His Highness the Archbishop of Besançon, he conducted the exorcisms on the spot for fourteen days; after he had called in several priests chosen by him, all persons of great piety and great merit, and moreover assigned to them Mr. Morel, formerly the city physician of Châlons, known for his science and experience; who all agreed in the same judgment concerning the matter, which the aforesaid Lord Bishop presented to us under the following points of view:

First, that all those virgins in their entirety, 18 in number, some secular, some ecclesiastical, and without excepting even one, appeared to him to have the gift of tongues; inasmuch as they always answered correctly to the Latin with which the exorcists addressed them, not from the ritual, and still less by prior agreement. Often they also expressed themselves in Latin, sometimes in whole periods, once or twice through formal speeches. One among them, Anne des Ecolos, called of the Purification, when one of the exorcists spoke Irish to her, testified that she understood him very well, and explained what was said to him several times in the French language. Secondly, that all or nearly all showed that they possessed a knowledge of the interior, and of the secret of thoughts when these were directed toward them; which showed itself especially in the inner commands that the exorcists gave them on many occasions, to which they in general obeyed very exactly, without these commands being translated into words or any external sign; concerning which the Lord Bishop himself made various experiments. \[Page 219\]

Thus among others in the person of Denise Parisot, maid of the General-Lieutenant von Auronne, to whose demon he, in the depths of his thoughts, had directed the command: to come to him, in order to allow himself to be exorcized. She came at once, although she lived in a distant quarter of the city, and said: that she had been commanded to present herself before him; an experiment which repeated itself with her several times. Further in the person of Sister Margaretha Janini, called of the Child Jesus, novice; who, when the exorcism was at an end, recited to him the command which he had imposed on the demon in the course of it. Even more in the person of Humberte Borthon, called of the holy Francis, to whom he, in the midst of her highest agitation, had given the order to prostrate herself at full length before the holy Sacrament with outstretched hands; a command which she fulfilled in the moment of its utterance with extraordinary zeal and great speed. The other clergymen who had been present there, according to his report, since the same thing occurred with them every day, had adopted it as the manner of making them obey, into their practice.

Thirdly, that they on various occasions had foretold future things, especially in regard to the maleficia and sorceries which one must find; not only at various places in the convent, where they were indeed really found; but also in the bodies of other sisters, with whom they had not previously spoken, and who then vomited them forth and expelled them from themselves exactly at the hour which those had determined for them. At times they had told the Holy Bishop, and some of his clergymen, very secret particulars in regard to their household affairs, and the time of his journey to Paris, which he himself had not even known; which things then turned out in truth just as stated, but could neither be guessed nor combined from the circumstances. Fourthly, that nearly all of them, especially at the height of their agitation, had shown a great aversion to all holy things, especially the sacraments of the Eucharist and Penance; so that sometimes on account of the violent resistance and outcries, which could only be subdued by commands directed to the demon, several hours were spent over such a confession.

Before Communion they were seized with convulsions and visibly involuntary movements; as soon as they received the holy Host, they cried out and howled terribly, and rolled on the ground; while the received Host always remained on the tip of the tongue, which they, at the command of the exorcist, stuck out or drew back; without, however, committing any irreverence against the holy Sacrament. This lasted sometimes half an hour, more or less; but when at last the received particle was swallowed, then she who had taken it remained immediately calm, and without remembrance of what had occurred. That further they had felt the most extraordinary aversions and fits of rage, at the approach of the relics of the saints, which they often recognized and named by name, before they had seen them, and without knowing anything of them. That furthermore nearly all, when the holy Bishop several times secretly laid hands on them, and without their being able to know it, had given to understand how they felt it; as they cried out: this hand is unbearable to them, it presses heavily, they would be burned by it! That finally at the height of the exorcism, especially during holy Mass, they had uttered blasphemies, and such frequent and terrible imprecations against God and his holy Mother, that one could not possibly hear them without horror; which, as may be supposed, could only proceed from the mouth of the demon. \[Page 220\]

Fifthly, that, when they were pressed to prove the presence of the demon through supernatural signs, they seemed to comply; among others, the maid Denise Parisot, who, when the Lord Bishop commanded her, caused the pulse of her right arm to stand completely still, while it continued undisturbed on the left; then the beating was transferred from the left to the right, while it now stood still on the left; all of which she executed with the utmost precision in the presence of several clerics and the physician, who examined and confirmed it. That the Sister of the Purification performed the same feat two or three times; both the one and the other in full health, and thus holding or releasing the pulse according to the command of the exorcist. That the Sister Margaretha Janini of the Child Jesus achieved the same, and at the exorcist's bidding inflated her breast to a monstrous height; but when he commanded a halt under the sign of the cross, she immediately caused it to subside: and this three times in succession with an astonishing efficacy, taking effect as rapidly as the word. That the Sister Lazara Arivey, called of the Resurrection, came to one of the clerics; carrying in her hand a coal of considerable length in full glow, without giving any sign of feeling the burn; and so several other effects of a similar nature, which cannot easily be set forth here in detail.

Sixthly, that at the mere command of the exorcist they sometimes fell into a wonderful insensibility; among others, Denise, who, when the Lord Bishop commanded the demon to withhold her senses, and the physician, to whom she expressly declared that she was entirely painless, thrust a needle under the nail of her finger, where, according to her own account, it shows itself most sensitive, immediately stated: that she felt not the slightest thing. When she was commanded: to hold back the blood, the needle was withdrawn without any blood following. But at the command to let it flow, it flowed forth at once in abundance; then holding it back again, when the command to halt was repeated. The same thing recurred a few days later on the person of the Sister of the Purification, whose skin on the arm one had wounded with a needle that was driven into her finger up to its head; without any pain or blood making itself felt, and without the sister appearing ill or faint; she rather always spoke, and urged those present to apply fire and iron, because she felt nothing of any of it. That some among them, especially the Sister of the Purification, when on a night in which, according to the assurance that the others had given the exorcist the day before, she was to be fetched away for the Sabbath, was prevented from leaving the cloister; at the hour of this alleged assembly suddenly fell into a kind of stupor and wonderful insensibility, which lasted five quarters of an hour and longer. All her senses were closed; she lay without movement, without speech, and without self-consciousness; her arms crossed on her breast, and so rigid that it was impossible to pull them apart; her eyes at first closed, and then opened, but held immovably fixed, and without power of sight; as was evident when one passed hands before her, and she did not twitch her eyelids like a dead or entirely insensible person. When she returned from this trance, she recounted: how she had been at the Sabbath in spirit, and all that she had seen there. \[Page 221\]

Seventhly, that they often, after several hours had been spent in conjurations and exorcisms, appeared to vomit up from the bottom of their stomachs certain foreign bodies, which they were accustomed to call maleficia and magic remedies of various kinds: pieces of wax, bones, hairs; besides pebbles of such size---according to our judgment broader and thicker than a silver thaler---so that it seemed difficult to us that they could be driven upward through the throat in a natural way. Finally, that the possessed one, among other things, after three hours of exorcisms and extraordinary exertions, expelled through her mouth a living frog or toad the breadth of a fist, and that the creature was immediately burned.

Eighthly, that the demons, by whom the girls claimed to be possessed, when pressed by the exorcisms to depart, appeared to give supernatural and convincing signs in the vicinity of the Most Holy Sacrament. When the bishop commanded them to depart from the possessed one, and as a sign thereof to break a pane which he indicated with his finger, the pane was broken. That Sister Humberthe Borthon was found completely and entirely healed on the day of the Presentation of the Virgin in 1661; and as a sign of her deliverance she vomited through her mouth a folded piece of taffeta, upon which in red script the name of Mary was written, and four other initial letters signifying St. Hubert and the blessed Francis de Sales. That the sister named of the Purification had been freed from several demons on the day of St. Gregory the Wonderworker; and as a sign thereof she gave forth through her mouth a piece of cloth in a circle of copper, upon which the name Gregory was written; and that the same one, on that same day of the Presentation, as a sign of another deliverance from several demons, caused the words Jesus, Mary, Joseph to appear in large letters, as if written with blood, on her bandage in an instant; while the exorcists had seen the bandage entirely white just a moment before.

Ninthly, that among the violent movements and postures which they made during the exorcism, some appeared so extraordinary that one had to judge they exceeded the strength of a girl; indeed, the powers of nature. That Sister Borthon, when commanded to adore the Most Holy Sacrament, threw herself to the ground, touching it only with the tip of her belly over the stomach; but with her head, feet, and hands, as well as the rest of her body, directed into the air. That the sister of the Resurrection practiced the same, and sometimes lay thus with her body bent into a circle; so that her soles touched her forehead. That Constantia and the possessed one were sometimes seen thrown to the ground, touching it only with the crown of the head and the feet, the entire rest of the body in the air, and that they walked about in this state. That all or nearly all, when they lay on their knees with their arms crossed over the stomach, turned themselves backward; so that the crown of the head connected with the soles of the feet, but the mouth kissed the earth, and with the tongue traced the sign of the cross on the ground. That some, among others Sister Catherine, during the exorcism appeared with the head thrown back, the eyes open; yet in such a way that, as the pupil was entirely hidden under the upper eyelid, one saw only the white in the eye, whereby she probably had lost the power of sight; an appearance that had been frightful to behold. That the possessed one, who was young and weak in appearance, when she was in agitation, with two fingers threw to the ground a vessel of a kind of marble, filled with holy water, and so heavy that two exceedingly strong persons would have had difficulty lifting it and removing it from its pedestal, with an ease that she might have used for a small stone. \[Page 222\]

That it has often happened to some and to others, in the heat of their attacks, to dash their heads against the wall or the ground; sometimes with such violent and hard blows that, in the natural order of things, they must have severely injured themselves with bloodshed; but that neither contusion, nor wound, nor any sign thereof appeared. Tenthly, that all these girls are of diverse stations: secular, novices, postulants, professed; further, young and more advanced in years; some from the city, others not; some of good and some of lowly origin; poor and rich; that this misfortune has already begun in the convent for ten years and more; that it is scarcely conceivable how, in so long a time, a scheme of deceit and subterfuge, among so many girls of such diverse dispositions and opposing interests, could have remained undiscovered; that in a sharp investigation and precise inquiry, the Lord Bishop found no one, whether in the convent or in the city, who did not speak to him most favorably of the innocence and blamelessness, both of the virgins and of the clerics who had worked before him in the exorcisms; and he testifies on his part that he recognized them in their conduct as exemplary, deserving, and pious persons: a testimony which he believes himself obliged to give in duty to truth and justice. To all this added the testimony of Mr. Morel, the physician, who was present at everything, and who assures that all these things surpass the bounds of nature, and can only proceed from the demon; so we believe, having weighed everything well, that all these extraordinary facts in those virgins go beyond the powers of human nature, and can only be wrought by the demon, who possesses and besets their bodies. That is our opinion. Given in Paris on the 20th of January 1662.

One sees with what circumspection these men proceeded, examining and weighing everything carefully; and we shall see who will have the forehead to contradict their testimony, and to declare respectable men as deceivers, or as deceived by the juggling tricks of the companions of a convent and its conniving spiritual directors, continued for more than ten years, whose good reputation is secured by the testimony of an entire city. But assuming the event to be true, since no one was found upon whom any suspicion of bewitchment rested, the evil must therefore have arisen within the convent itself through immediate communication, either simultaneously in all, or also in one or more, and then passed from one to the other through epidemic contagion; until finally the entire community was seized. Since they drew it upon themselves on the Sabbath, it has been a true obsession that overtook them; but since none among them was found from whom one could truly have suspected that she had first given occasion to the evil through her own fault; it has therefore come upon them as a judgment, and it has been an obsession that yet again emerged in all the forms of a possession; which therefore here proceeded from a source of contagion lying entirely outside the circle of the human realm. \[Page 223\]

Such obsessions differ, except for the Sabbath, in none of the other phenomena from those which the possessions exhibit; but they are at the same time, except for goal and intention, otherwise in all things equal to the symptoms of higher ecstasies. The gift of languages, the beholding of another's thoughts, the hearing of the commands of the exorcist from afar, the knowledge of holy things, of the sacraments, of relics and consecrations, here expressing itself as loathing and horror, the power of the will over the unfree ganglionic life, invulnerability to fire, painlessness and closure of the senses, the stopping and flowing of the blood at will, the drawing in of the whole body into the form of a circle, or successively into the forms of two half-circles divided from one another and turned toward each other: all of this we have already seen mutatis mutandis in the saints just as well. That circle which the one formed would, had the exorcist so willed, have rolled itself just as much in the circular streaming of the forces, toward any arbitrary point on the radial line; as the holy Peter of Alcántara did it voluntarily in his ecstasies toward the Most Holy Sacrament.

These events are proven in the saints by the most unimpeachable testimonies; they are proven here now in the possessed by equally unimpeachable witnesses; the facts confirm one another just as much, and here as always the devil, so far as it lies in his power, must against his will bear witness for the higher truth. All of this is in nature, for it is executed with natural forces; but it is also above nature, for the ground to which these forces attach themselves lies beyond the region of ordinary life. Next to this, the casting forth of objects designated by certain names seems still to point to jugglery and deception. So much is certainly true: these things did not write themselves, the devil did not write them either; therefore it was the nuns who did it. But they did not do it in waking senses, with the intention of deception, but rather as they were beside themselves, in the properly negative demonic ecstasy; in it they also swallowed the written things, which alone would have been possible in such a state. \[Page 224\]

As the exorcism now called forth a kind of positive, anti-demonic ecstasy, all the movements of the negative ones reversed themselves, thus also the peristaltic movements; and they had to cast forth again what they had previously swallowed down. In all these proceedings, the saint stands to the one under whose obedience he has placed himself, and the possessed to the exorcist, in the same relation as the magnetized stands to the magnetizer; only that this natural relation there passes over into a higher or deeper region of things through intensification, here through depression, according to the positivity or negativity of the exponents. It is otherwise remarkable that the witnesses of this proceeding, who believed in the bodily departure, in the Sabbath, had the departing ones watched at the appointed hour, and now found them as if caught in a vision. The possibility of such a departure in very rare cases is, as we have seen, by no means to be denied; but had the investigators been able to occupy themselves with the matter longer than fourteen days, they would, as can scarcely be doubted, always have found only the vision. What was thus found in Auronne had also earlier been discerned in Louviers. There the Sister du Saint Esprit was possessed by Dagon; this one once wound himself around the girl's body in a threefold coil, like a writhing snake, by twisting the region of the stomach on the body to one side like a loop, the feet to the opposite side, but elongating the head toward the shoulders, so that she had the appearance of a knotted coil of snakes. \[Page 225\]

As for the children, in the Basque country some two thousand of them had been found, who, according to their statements, had been to the Sabbath. They had all confessed: if a sorceress wanted to lead them there, she would merely pass her hand over their face or head; immediately thereafter they would find themselves wholly confused, and as if out of themselves; but they did not say that the hands had been anointed. Sometimes, they protested, the women would give them an apple to eat, or a piece of black millet bread; after they had eaten it, they would become entirely defenseless, and then it would not fail---they would come the following night to fetch them. Even if they were then held fast in the arms of their elders and siblings, no one could awaken them. Such was the unanimous testimony of 2--300 children who were examined on the matter.

Johanna du Hard, 56 years old, had testified: when she had gone out of the church with a professed sorceress named Chorrozique, the latter had touched her arm, and she had immediately become as if dead. Corneille Brolu, 12 years old, deposed: that once, in 1608 during the fast at St. Jean de Luz, the sorceress Marie Martin had passed her hand over his head; and thereafter, in the following night, in the form of a cat, had taken him from his bed, out from the midst of two other boys; and had led him to Lecohanda, that is, to the great lake, where the Sabbath was held. Since that woman had died, he had not gone there for a month; until another took charge of him and led him there again. Since then he had been disenchanted, in that the woman whom they had summoned to justify herself---because she had not white but, like all her kind, red blood---had had some drops of it drawn, and with it a belt had been smeared. In the Swedish Elfdale as well, the children were awakened from sleep and taken there, with or against their will. If they betrayed it to anyone, they were harshly beaten at the following Sabbath; signs of this, however, were seldom to be discovered. Upon their return, the children usually looked quite weak, pale, and battered, and could scarcely recover the next day. They therefore often sought to save themselves before being led away, and when it began to come upon them, they would lie in the arms of their elders. These would sit by them and watch over them whole nights through; and as soon as they noticed an unusual pallor in them, they would shake them violently, but it helped nothing.

They also noticed that their breast became entirely cold; they also stuck a burning light into their hair, but it did not ignite. Their state of being away from themselves lasted sometimes half an hour, a full hour, or even two hours; and when the children came back to themselves, they lamented and wept most piteously, and begged forgiveness to the utmost of their ability, as much as they could. This was solemnly declared on oath before the court by two old men, who wished to call all the residents of the village as witnesses; for their children had mostly all experienced the same thing. Those grips of the witches were magnetic grips, which transferred the state of the one grasping into the one grasped. The state was, from the natural side, a magnetism; an inner awakening of the ganglia of the lower body, connected with the closure of the senses, the concentration of life in that region, and thus a cooling of the lung system; as it all showed itself in those Nordic children. But since the magnetism was at the same time of a demonic nature, the Sabbath had necessarily to be evoked in the circle of visions. \[Page 233\]

Demonic Possession of the Nuns of Quercy.verbatim:
Thus Massäus says: In the year 1491, around the feast of Peter's Chair, the demons began to inhabit and possess the convent of the nuns of Quercy (Quercetensium), and to torment its inhabitants most cruelly for four years and four months. One saw them frequently running through the fields like dogs, flying in the air like birds, climbing trees in the manner of cats, hanging from the branches, imitating the voices of various animals, penetrating secrets, and prophesying future things. \[Page 243\]

So often Heinrich, Bishop of Cambrai, or Aegidius Nettetet, Dean of his church, both pious men, set out for exorcism, they knew it beforehand, and cried: The one with the horns is again on the way to threaten us. After all manner of means had been applied, which were sought out from everywhere, their names were brought to Rome and read out by Alexander VI on Maundy Thursday under the Mass; but without any effect. Johanna Potier, who was held to be the beginning of the evil, had been in confidential relations with the demon from her ninth year onward, and this one accused her in the convent: that she had gone to Communion 434 times unworthily; which statement, however, since he is a liar from the beginning, cannot be trusted. She was led to Cambrai and died in the dungeon on St. Martin's Day; the others were freed in June after four years of possession. Joh. Molinet in his Belgian chronicle for the year 1490 confirms these accounts, adding: that the evil had passed from one to the other innocents. The demons had given themselves out as angels of light who belonged to the hierarchy of the Seraphim, and had at last been driven out by the Dean of Cambrai. He had carried the Eucharist to the sick, and set the demons the condition: if it were nothing but bread, then it might by no means disturb them in their possession; but if the body of the Lord, then they must withdraw from the possessed.
